Are Plastic Cups Food Safe? PET, PP and FDA Food-Grade Explained

Article Quick Facts

PET Material
Food-grade, recycling code 1
PP Material
Food-grade, recycling code 5
PET Temp Limit
Cold only, up to ~60°C
PP Temp Limit
Hot & cold, up to ~100°C

What "Food-Grade" Actually Means

Food-grade means the material is manufactured from food-contact-approved resin and is intended for direct contact with beverages. Both PET and PP used for beverage cups are standard food-contact plastics. The key for buyers is to confirm the resin grade and to match the material to the drink temperature, since using a cup outside its temperature range is the most common safety mistake.

PET vs PP: Food-Safety Profile

A material-level comparison to inform your food-safety and sourcing decisions.

PropertyPETPP
Recycling code1 (PETE)5 (PP)
Food contactFood-grade resinFood-grade resin
Temperature useCold only (~60°C max)Hot & cold (~100°C max)
Typical drinksIced coffee, juice, bobaHot tea, hot coffee, hot & cold
ClarityCrystal clearClear to frosted

Temperature Is a Safety Boundary

The single most important safety rule is temperature. PET is engineered for cold and ambient drinks up to about 60°C and will deform if filled with hot liquid — so it should never be used for hot beverages. PP tolerates up to about 100°C, making it the correct choice for hot tea and coffee. Insulated paper cups are the other hot-drink option.

What to Confirm With Any Supplier

Before ordering, confirm the resin is food-grade, ask which market certifications apply to your destination, and match each cup to its intended drink temperature. A responsible supplier will state the material grade and temperature range for every cup line rather than making blanket claims.

Article FAQs

Are PET and PP cups food safe?

Yes, when produced from food-grade resin and used within their temperature range. PET is for cold drinks up to ~60°C; PP handles hot and cold up to ~100°C.

What do the recycling numbers mean?

PET cups are code 1 (the most widely recycled plastic) and PP cups are code 5. Both are food-contact plastics; recyclability depends on local facilities.

Why can't I put hot coffee in a PET cup?

PET softens above about 60°C and will deform. For hot drinks use PP cups or insulated paper cups, both of which tolerate higher temperatures.
